## 4. The specification, comment by comment

1. **The closure.** `Specification/basic/traits.tex:259-275`: a trait that comprises
   `OrganicMolecule` and `InorganicMolecule` may not be extended by a third trait ("the following
   trait declaration is not allowed"), and `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:549-570` draws
   the consequence that every subtype of a comprising trait is a subtype of one of the listed
   traits; so `comprises { ZZ }` is false while `Integral[\I\]` (.fss:615) extends `AnyIntegral`
   directly. `traits.tex:231-235` states it outright (the listed traits "are exactly the traits
   that immediately extend" the trait), but in a `\note`, which a release build suppresses
   (`Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:35-37`) — the ground on which item 2 below sets aside the
   `aggregate.tex` margin notes — so it corroborates and does not decide. The
   true statement names every instantiation of `Integral`, and the grammar has no way to say so:
   `extends` takes `TraitTypeWheres`, a type with an optional `where` (`traits.tex:76-83`), but
   `comprises` takes only `TraitTypes` (`:88`), and the parser matches
   (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/NoNewlineHeader.rats:96-139`). That is what the
   team's `NOT YET` says; the note says it and nothing more, and promises no checker change.
2. **`Array3`.** An `excludes` clause means no trait can extend both (`traits.tex:218-222`); types
   that exclude have subtypes that exclude (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:163-164`);
   tuple types exclude if a pair of their elements do (`:276-277`); and "without coercion,
   incompatibility is equivalent to exclusion" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:182`),
   which makes two declarations with incompatible parameter types a valid overloading (`:212-216`).
   So an operator one of whose parameters is an `Array3` never overlaps `AdditiveGroup[\T\]`'s
   `+(self, other: T)` (.fss:333), whatever `T` is, because `T` extends `AnyAdditiveGroup`. The
   price is the clause's plain meaning: no type extends both `Array3` and `AdditiveGroup`. `Array1`
   and `Array2` cannot carry the same exclusion because `Vector` (.fss:2193-2194) and `Matrix`
   extend them and are additive groups, and `traits.tex:222` forbids extending two excluding
   traits. On which future rank 3 should have, the specification is silent: its prose makes a one-
   and two-dimensional numeric array a vector and a matrix
   (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:150-166`) and says nothing of rank 3 beyond
   indexing. The margin notes beside that passage (`aggregate.tex:152-162`, which a release build
   suppresses, `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:35-37`) contemplate `Matrix` types of rank
   `k > 1`, with an editor's dissent; they are draft text, not the standard, and they lean toward
   the future the clause forecloses (the skeptic's F5). The choice is Pavol's, taken 2026-09-21.
   The "future one" use is already gated:
   `ProjectFortress/test_library/ArrayOperatorVocabulary.fsi:6-7` declares the plane-wise `+`
   between a `Matrix` and an `Array3`, and `ProjectFortress/tests/ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary.fss:23-24`
   checks it. The fixture declares two `+`, which is ledger row 341's trigger (two or more
   declarations of one name with a trait-typed operand in the non-self position,
   `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md` row 341), so the interpreter does check the pair against the
   library's: on a cold cache it refuses it without the clause, against `AdditiveGroup`'s
   `+(self, other: T)` (.fss:333; `probes/skeptic/SkArray3Exclusion.txt` A2 and A4), and a warm
   cache passes it (A3, A5). The rung's first gated run (`probes/gated-tests-postedit.txt:16-26`)
   followed other post-edit walks on the worktree's caches, so it met a warm cache and said nothing
   about the clause; the branch's own evidence is the cold run of the repair round, in which the
   fixture loads on this branch's library and prints its nine lines (`probes/gated-cold-postrepair.txt`).
   The static checker gives no evidence either way: on the fixture's vocabulary its overloading
   check crashes on the `nat` parameters (`STypesUtil.scala:557`), and on a `nat`-free rendering at
   fixed sizes it reports 0 errors with the clause and without it
   (`probes/skeptic/SkA3Concrete-checker.txt`). The number case is different. The scalar block
   holds the (number, `Array`) slot for every `Array3`, since `Array3` extends
   `StandardMutableArrayType` (.fss:2666-2669), which extends `Array[\E,I\]` (.fss:1991-1992); a user
   pair of `+` between an `RR64` and an `Array3` is refused on a cold cache against the block's
   `opr +[\T extends Number, I\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T)` (.fss:4509) with the clause (B1) and without
   it (B3), and loads either way once the block's two `+` are removed (B5, B6). That is why
   comment 2 now names the lower-rank case only (decision 7). Under the static-parameter sentence
   (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-104`: "it is an error for their static parameters to
   differ") the fixture's `+` and the number pair would both be errors whatever the exclusion;
   that sentence is Pavol's to decide (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:164`), and the
   comment says nothing of it.
3. **The unsized result, and 4. the reversed `-`.** The specification's prose on arithmetic
   between an array and a scalar is `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:143-147`:
   multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is juxtaposition, and division of a matrix or
   vector by a scalar may be written `/`. It names no operand order and no result type, and it
   says nothing of `+`, `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` between an array and a scalar (the grep in the
   provenance block), so both comments record library decisions, taken on 2026-09-21 as the
   explainer's defaults 3a-A and 3b-A. Comment 4's statement that the juxtaposition pairs commute
   agrees with the passage. What the comments state as fact was
   measured under `walk` (`probes/CommentedDecls.fss`, capture `probes/CommentedDecls-postedit.txt`):
   `3 - x` is `[0#2][ 2 1 ]` for `x: ZZ32[2] = [1 2]` and `x - 3` is `[0#2][ -2 -1 ]`; `m + 1.0`
   and `0.0 MAX m` are `Matrix[\RR64,2,2\]` at run time, `1.0 - v` a `Vector[\RR64,3\]`, and
   `10.0 - t` an `Array3` (the `replica` claim: .fss:2139-2140, :2401-2402, :2770-2772). The gated
   `ProjectFortress/tests/ArrayScalarExtension.fss:23` and `:45` already pin the reversed `-`
   (`(1.0 - v)[0] = 2.0`, `(1 - iv)[0] = 2`). The precedents' commutativity: every Vector and
   Matrix scalar pair calls the same `me.scale(other)` in both orders (.fss:2271-2281, :2648-2658).

The library's scalar extension generalised and its exclusion tower closed

Four sites in Library/FortressLibrary.fss, mirrored in .fsi:

- :4496-4504 (api :2540-2547), the block that was :4493-4517: the integer scalar-extension block
  `opr + - MIN MAX (Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], ZZ32)` becomes eight generic
  declarations `[\T extends Number, I\]`, both operand orders, on the
  precedent of the `T extends Number` array operators at :2264-2279 and
  :2624-2637.
- :612 (api :409): `trait AnyIntegral extends { QQ } comprises { ZZ }`
  closes the numeric tower's one open comprises link; the api already
  closes `ZZ` at :536.
- :327-328 (api :250-251): the `AnyMultiplicativeRing` placeholder pattern
  of :338-339 (api :262-263) applied to `AdditiveGroup` -- a marker `trait
  AnyAdditiveGroup end` that `AdditiveGroup` extends.
- :2669 (api :1659): `Array3 excludes { Number, String, AnyAdditiveGroup,
  AnyMultiplicativeRing }`.

Why the tower has to be closed for the generic block to load beside
`AdditiveGroup.+` and `StandardTotalOrder.MAX`: the interpreter makes a
trait with a `comprises` clause exclude whatever every leaf of its
transitive comprises excludes (FType.java:281-297,
FTypeTrait.java:68-78). `ZZ32`'s leaves are the objects `Int` and
`IntLiteral`, which is why the shipped ground block loads; `RR64`'s leaves
included `AnyIntegral`, a trait with no comprises clause, which excludes
nothing, so nothing above `RR64` excluded the symbolic bound of a library
operator's type variable and the generic block over `T extends Number`
would be refused. With `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` the tower is closed.
The marker trait and the `Array3` clause do the same for a user operator
whose non-self operand is an `Array3`.

The two tests, each run from an empty FORTRESS_CACHES, red on the tree
before this edit and green after:

- tests/ArrayScalarExtension.fss -- 24 checks of `+ - MIN MAX` in both
  operand orders over an `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, a `Matrix` and an
  `Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]`, the last pinning the shipped block's behaviour,
  which no test asserted. Before: "Failed to find any matching overload,
  args = (__DefaultVector[\RR64,3\],1.0)".
- tests/ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary.fss with the api fixture
  test_library/ArrayOperatorVocabulary.{fsi,fss} -- a user vocabulary over
  the standard arrays that must load beside the library's operators: two
  `MINMAX` over `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, the plane-wise `+` between a
  `Matrix` and an `Array3` in both orders, and two `juxtaposition`
  declarations at rank 3. Before: "... has a parameter with generic type,
  at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" against
  `StandardTotalOrder.MINMAX`. One user declaration of an operator name is
  not checked against the library's (gap-ledger row 341), so the fixture
  declares two of each, as the programs that hit this do; the fixture goes
  in test_library/, the fourth entry on fortress.source.path, which is
  where this corpus keeps the apis its tests import.

Gate on this tree, caches wiped first: ant testSystem 384 tests (382 plus
these two), 0 failures; ant testFast 1,409 tests, 0 failures.

## What landed

Two tokens, one in each of the interpreter's two float `round` natives:

- `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Float.java:384`, in `class Round extends R2L` (`:382-386`): `return Math.round(x);` becomes `return (long) Math.rint(x);`.
- `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/RR32.java:326`, in `class Round extends F2L` (`:324-328`): `return (long) Math.round((double) x);` becomes `return (long) Math.rint((double) x);`.

And two new interpreter tests:

- `ProjectFortress/tests/RoundHalfEvenRungR.fss`: 21 assertions and a closing `PASS`, the rung's gate.
- `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRoundNearTieNumeral.fss`, added in the repair round: four assertions of the specification's answers for four numerals near a tie, an expected failure today. It is the home-2 gate of the numeral defect the first skeptic measured (see "The numeral defect measured by the first skeptic").

`testSystem` goes from 384 to 386 tests (see "What else it touches").

Nothing else was edited: not `Floor`, `Ceiling`, `ICeiling`, `IFloor`, `Truncate` or `RawBits`, not the declarations in `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:190-191` and `:341-342`, and not the compiled path.

## Differentials

1. **Walk before against walk after:** the probe pair above.
2. **Walk after against compiled.** `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/probes/RoundHalfEvenCompiledProbe.fss` is the compiled twin of the probe's eleven RR64 `Float` lines, built the same way. It was run after the full library-order cache rebuild, and its capture is `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/probes/RoundHalfEvenCompiledProbe.txt`, compile exit 0 and run exit 0. Once the compiled path's extra space after `=` is dropped (its juxtaposition spacing, ledger row 76), all eleven lines are identical to the walk-after lines (`diff` empty). Against walk-before they differ on the four ties. So the divergence of row 329 is closed for RR64 at the ties and nothing new diverges at the edges. The probe's comment (`RoundHalfEvenCompiledProbe.fss:5-6`) says the `RR32` lines have no compiled twin. That is wrong: a typed binding such as `h32: RR32 = 2.5` builds an `RR32` on the compiled path through `trait RR32`'s `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:989`), as the first skeptic's `probes/skeptic/SkRoundComp.fss:24-29` does. Its capture, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/probes/skeptic/SkRoundComp.txt:15-17`, gives `8388606`, `8388608` and `2`, the same as `walk` after the edit (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/probes/skeptic/SkRoundWalk-after.txt:19-21`). The comment is left as captured.
3. **The new test file on the compiled path**, which is where a future full-corpus ladder run (`tests/*.fss`) will put it: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/probes/RoundHalfEvenRungR-compiled.txt`, `fortress compile` exit 255, `File RoundHalfEvenRungR.fss has 28 errors`, all at typecheck. There are 21 `Could not check call to function assert` errors, because the compiled prelude has no `assert(Any, Any, String)`; the argument types it reports, `(ZZ64, IntLiteral, String)`, show that `round` itself typechecked on every line, RR32 included. The other 7 are `Could not check call to function narrow`, because the compiled prelude's `narrow` is `ZZ64->ZZ32` and `NN64->NN32` only. The RR32 `round` lines typecheck because `trait RR64` has `coerce(x: RR32)` and RR32 widens exactly to RR64, whose `round` is the `rint` of shape 2, so the compiled answer for RR32 is also half to even.

Classification (decision): neither of the two refusals in differential 3 is a defect of `round`. Both are names absent from the compiler prelude, which by Pavol's decision takes no new declarations and is deleted at the switch-over (`POSITIONS.md:45`), so no ledger row is opened for them. The alternative was a row for each; I rejected it because a row whose only repair is forbidden by a standing decision names no fix. The `assert` refusal is already the ladder's first error in 4 `tests/` files (`explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv`, `first_error` column). This file will add a 382nd `tests` row, at typecheck, to the next full-corpus baseline. It is a new file, not a move.

| 360 | a numeral with a radix point is rounded, floored, ceiled and truncated as its nearest double, not as the rational it denotes, on both paths: `round(2.50000000000000001)` is 2 and `floor(2.99999999999999999)` is `3.0`, not 3 and 2 | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | library gap vs spec (library) | `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex`, "Literals"; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers" | `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRoundNearTieNumeral.fss` | climb batch 3 rung R's skeptic | At 052a7c3fe, under walk `object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:194`) declares none of the four, so `RR64`'s bodies run over `asFloat(self)`, `Double.valueOf` of the text (the interpreter's `FFloatLiteral.java:39-40`); compiled, the prelude has no ℚ and `RR64`'s `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` makes the double (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:932`). `2.50000000000000001`, `2.49999999999999999` and `2.5` share one double, and want 3, 2, 2. ## The test, first

`ProjectFortress/tests/RoundHalfEvenRungR.fss` is a component exporting `Executable`, as `ProjectFortress/tests/roundBug.fss` is. The directory has no `.test` files (`FileTests.java:710-711`, `InterpreterTest`): a test there passes when `Driver.runProgram` returns without an exception.

Its 21 assertions fall into three groups:

- **RR64 through a literal** (`:7-15`), which is `trait Number`'s route to `Float$Round`: the four ties the brief names, `round(2.5) = 2`, `round(-3.5) = -4`, `round(0.5) = 0` and `round(-1.5) = -2`; two ties on which half-up and half-to-even agree, `3.5 → 4` and `-2.5 → -2`; and three non-ties, `2.4 → 2`, `2.6 → 3` and `-2.6 → -3`. The ties that agree catch a body that rounds half down or toward zero, and the non-ties catch truncation.
- **RR64 through a `Float`** built with `SQRT`, as `roundBug.fss:19` builds its operand (`:17-21`): the four ties and `3.5 → 4`.
- **RR32** made with `narrow`, as `ProjectFortress/tests/testRR32.fss:19-20` makes one (`:23-36`): the four ties, `4.5 → 4` and `-4.5 → -4` (the brief's pair), and `3.5 → 4`.

Each tie line's message carries its citation, `numbers.tex:470-472, ledger row 329`, and the file's one comment line points here.

**Decision: the comparison form.** The brief asks for the form of `ProjectFortress/library_tests/RR64FunctionsRungF.fss:87-90`, which is `assert(round(twoHalf).asZZ32, two32, "round 2.5 = 2")`, and asks that it survive row 330's change of the declared type to ℤ. That exact form cannot be written in the interpreter world: `asZZ32` is declared nowhere in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss` (grep, no hit). It is the compiled prelude's conversion, needed there because that prelude is flat.

I used instead the interpreter's own form for the same assertion, `assert(round(x), 2, "…")`. That is the three-argument `assert(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg: Any...)` of `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:296-300`, which compares with `=/=`. It is how `RationalTest.fss:398-440` asserts ℚ's `round`, whose declared type is already `ZZ` (`FortressLibrary.fss:592`), so the form is shown working against a ℤ declaration. The test names `ZZ64` nowhere, so row 330's change touches none of its text.

The alternative was a typed binding such as `r: ZZ64 = round(x)`. It would pin today's declared type and break on row 330, which is what the brief asked me to avoid. What the test deliberately does not assert is the result's type; that is row 330's.

With the import lines at `:14-18` (`java.util.List`, `compiler.runtimeValues.FValue` added in the repair round, `Naming`, `RTHelpers`), 44 lines against the base.
17:- Unchanged on purpose: `FValue.toString` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:25-27`) stays `this.asString().toString()`. For a class that declares a `toString` of its own, the default `asString` answers that `toString`; for every generated class whose Fortress declarations include no zero-argument member named `toString`, the Java `toString()Ljava/lang/String;` resolves to `FValue`'s (codegen defines no method of that descriptor: `grep -rn '"toString"' compiler/ runtimeSystem/` finds only calls, `CodeGen.java:2108` on a `StringBuilder` and `environments/TopLevelEnvGen.java:625` in the interpreter's environment classes) and is `this.asString().toString()`, the type name. So a Java caller's `toString()` of a value whose `asString` is this default shows what `println` shows, on every class but one kind. The grep cannot see a Java method codegen names after a Fortress declaration: a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` (method, getter or field) is emitted as `toString()Lfortress/CompilerBuiltin$String;` (`probes/skeptic/skeptic2-overflow-cycle.txt:8`), which `Class.getMethod("toString")` returns first, so `hasOwnToString` answers true for it and the default still overflows; that is item 13 of "Defects and their homes", measured by the second skeptic. `asDebugString` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:353`) stays `self.asString`; `stringOps.asString` and its `jAsString` import stay (see Decisions).
52:**The finding.** The skeptic measured that the rung's first native changed two renderings that already worked: on the rung tree `x: RR32 = 1.5; println(x)` printed `RR32` and `[RR32]` where the base tree and walk print `1.5` and `[1.5]`, and a `StringVector` holding `a`, `b` printed `StringVector` where the base default printed `[a b ]` (`probes/skeptic/differentials.txt:207-208`, `:214-217`; walk `:222-223`). The cause: `FRR32` and `FStringVector` are the only 2 of the 17 value classes in `compiler/runtimeValues/` whose Fortress trait declares no `asString` (`trait RR32`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:988-990`; `trait StringVector`, `:1150-1155`) and whose Java class declares none either (`FRR32.java`; `FStringVector.java:34` spells it `asSring`). I re-tabulated all 17 (a Java `asString()`, else the line of the trait's `getter asString`): only these two have neither. So the base default `jAsString(self)` (`a.toString()`) reached their own `toString`, and the rung's `jTypeName(self)` did not. `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:117-122` (read `:100-140`) settles it against the rung tree: `RR32` does not textually represent `1.5`. It also broke the batch record's interop rule (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:134`), and made the first report's sentence "a Java caller's `toString()` of a Fortress object now shows what `println` shows" false for these two classes.
56:**Where the judge's native was wrong against the source.** JUDGE.md section 5 step 1 gives the helper as `hasOwnToString(Class<?> c)`. With it, `ant compileAll` succeeds and the library rebuild fails in `CompilerBuiltin`: `java.lang.Error: No Fortress type (yet) for foreign Java type descriptor 'Ljava/lang/Class;'` from `FortressMethodAdapter.toImplFFFF` (`probes/judge-shape-wrapper-error.txt:6-8`). The native-wrapper generator reads the whole imported class (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:53`, `cr.accept(fa, 0)`) and wraps every method except `<init>`, `<clinit>` and those with bytes, shorts or arrays in the descriptor (`FortressMethodAdapter.java:215-225`, `SignatureParser.java:45-74`), private ones included, and throws for a parameter type with no Fortress counterpart (`FortressMethodAdapter.java:250-258`). Every private helper in an imported `nativeHelpers` class already has a mappable signature (`stringOps.fortressTypeName(String)`, `simpleIntLiteralArith.toBigInteger(IntLiteral)` and `fromBigInteger(BigInteger)`, `simpleIntArith.intCautiousNonNegativeMul(int, int)`, `simpleChar.charToHexString(int)`, `DeterministicRandom`'s three); the one with an unmappable type, `systemHelper.setFinalStatic(Field, Object)` (`systemHelper.java:25`), is in a class no Fortress source imports. So `hasOwnToString` takes the value, `fortress.AnyType.Any a`, and reads `a.getClass()` itself (`stringOps.java:79-81`); the logic is the judge's.
78:- **The reverse count, which the repaired defect raises.** Of the 17 value classes, 2 relied on the old default reaching their own `toString`, because neither their trait nor their Java class has an `asString`: `FRR32` (`FRR32.java:19`) and `FStringVector` (`FStringVector.java:24-30`). The other 15 have an `asString` at one level or the other (Java: `FFloatLiteral`, `FIntLiteral`, `FNN32`, `FRR64`, `FString`, `FZZ32`, `FZZ32Vector`; trait only: `FBoolean` `CompilerBuiltin.fss:1006`, `FCharacter` `:1061`, `FJavaBufferedReader` `:1158`, `FJavaBufferedWriter` `:1172`, `FJavaString` `:419`, `FNN64` `:821`, `FZZ` `:519`, `FZZ64` `:580`). The first round asked the forward question only; `defaultAsString` answers both.
79:- **A private helper in an imported native class.** Every one found has a Fortress-mappable signature (listed in "The repair round"), which is why `hasOwnToString` takes the value.
134:12. **The native-wrapper generator refuses an imported class with any method, private ones included, whose signature has a type with no Fortress counterpart** (measured in this round, JUDGE.md's `hasOwnToString(Class<?> c)`) — home 3, row 368 (provisional 359), because the specification's prose is silent on `import java` altogether (`grep -rln 'import java\|foreign' Specification/basic Specification/basic-lib` prints nothing). The adapter wraps every method of the class (`FortressMethodAdapter.java:215-225`), a private method cannot be imported, and the error names no method (`probes/judge-shape-wrapper-error.txt:6`). Worked around in this rung by giving the helper a mappable parameter.
135:13. **An object that declares or inherits a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` still overflows the stack on the compiled path** (the second skeptic's; row 321's one open case) — home 2, `compiler_tests/XXXFortToStringRungS.fss` with `XXXFortToStringRungS.test` (`run`, `run_out_contains=REACHED`) and `FortToStringRungSLink.test` (`link`), the second skeptic's proposal copied byte for byte from `probes/skeptic/proposed/` at the gather. The base tree overflowed on the same programs through `jAsString`, so it is not a regression. `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:19-22` and `:117-122` make the program legal and give every object a `toString`. The pair was shown red on a stand-in fix and back to an expected failure after the restore (`probes/skeptic/skeptic2-standin-fix.txt`), and run again at the gather on the merged tree (`probes/gather/fort-tostring-xxx.txt`).

1. **Row 321, the rendering cycle** — home 1, repaired. Its assertions are the 18 `assert` lines of `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS.fss:21-48`, each message carrying "ledger row 321" (the last also `FException.java:22-23`). They cover the entry points the row names that a test can reach: `println` (`:18-20`, checked by `run_out_contains=PASS` reaching `:49`), concatenation (`:33`), the prelude singletons `Nothing` and `None` (`:34-35`), and a `throw` of an object with no `asString` reaching its handler (`:42-48`). The transactional entry is gated already by `compiler_tests/AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`, which passes on the repaired tree (`probes/gated-spot-postrepair.txt:3-10`).
2. **The void, tuple and arrow spellings** — home 1: in the native and asserted at `DefaultRenderRungS.fss:27-32`.
3. **`RR32` and `StringVector` values rendered as their type name** (the skeptic's, introduced by the rung's first native) — home 1, repaired in this round: `DefaultRenderRungS.fss:36-41`, failing before the repair (`probes/test-prerepair.txt:11`), passing after (`probes/test-postedit.txt:10-15`), biting under mutation (`probes/mutation-owntostring.txt:17`). `objects.tex:117-122` settles it.

Walk prints `a Box: Box` (article + `ilkName` + `": "` + `asString`, `FortressBuiltin.fss:42-47`), the compiled path `Box` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:353` is `self.asString`). The specification's prose never names `asDebugString`, `asExprString` or `ilkName` (`grep -rn 'asExprString\|asDebugString\|ilkName' Specification/basic Specification/basic-lib` prints nothing, rc=1, re-run in this round), so this is the home for a silent specification, not a choice of convenience; the batch record keeps the repair out of this rung because `not_working_library_tests/Comparison1.fss:33-36` asserts `U.asDebugString = "Unordered"`. Probe: `probes/judgement-probes-both-paths.txt`. The gated test asserts nothing about `asDebugString`.
5. **`asExprString` diverges between the paths** (the skeptic's) — home 3, an addition to row 363, for the same reason: the prose is silent (the grep above). The specification settles it: with a string on the left, juxtaposition "conventionally performs string concatenation" (`Specification/basic/operators/intro.tex:68-70`, read `:50-76`), and string concatenation is `||` with no separator (`Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:75-79`, read `:65-95`); `juxtameaning.tex:103-105` makes `"<" Box(1) ">"` legal. ## 1. What the rung did

The brief is section 2, "B. The compiled path", of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md` (lines 25-37), with Pavol's riders as set at launch: siblings = with, signed narrow = truncates (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, B's tail).

- **(a) Row 335, compiled half.** `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` call four new natives with the smart-shift rule (`intBitLeftShift`/`intBitRightShift`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:353-362`; `longBitLeftShift`/`longBitRightShift`, `simpleLongArith.java:322-331`), bound at `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:72-73` and `:198-199` and called from the bodies at `:647-648` (`ZZ64`) and `:736-737` (`ZZ32`). A count at or beyond the width gives `0` for a left shift and the replicated sign for a right shift; in range, the machine shift, bits shifted out falling off; a negative count shifts the other way by its magnitude, saturating the same way, with the most negative count tested before any negation. `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` are unchanged.
- **(c) Row 333, and the siblings under the rider.** All sixteen `x==(-x)` guards of the two files are gone. Twelve now test `Integer.MIN_VALUE`/`Long.MIN_VALUE`: row 333's six (`simpleIntArith.java:80`, `:85`, `:90`; `simpleLongArith.java:80`, `:85`, `:90`) and six saturating siblings (`simpleIntArith.java:274`, `:279`, `:284`; `simpleLongArith.java:249`, `:254`, `:259`). The four guards in `longOverflowingMul` and `longSaturatingMul` were replaced by `Math.multiplyExact` (`simpleLongArith.java:70-76`, `:239-245`); the saturating one returns the file's existing sign formula `((a^b) >> 63) ^ Long.MAX_VALUE` on overflow. So zero answers `0` everywhere it was wrong (`|0|`, `-0`, `0 DIV -1`, `DOTMINUS 0`, every zero factor on `ZZ64`), and `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` on `ZZ64`, which multiply by the quotient, no longer throw on a zero quotient; the minimum still overflows or saturates. `multiplyExact` also repairs a second defect this rung measured: `-2^32 · 2^31`, which is `Long.MIN_VALUE`, used to throw (`probes/IntSemTable-compiled-before.txt:52`).
- **(d) Row 346, compiled half.** `ZZ64.narrow` is `jLongWrappingToInt(self)` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`) and `NN64.narrow` goes through `jLongWrappingToUnsignedInt` (`:879`), both imported before this rung and unused (`:51`, `:96`). Rung W's five throw assertions are reversed to the low-32-bit answers (`ProjectFortress/library_tests/IntConversionsRungW.fss:43-45`, `:63-64`) and its two helpers, which nothing else used, are removed. The getter `asZZ32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:581`) keeps its throw.
- No declaration was added or changed; `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` is untouched. The comment at `ProjectFortress/library_tests/IntegralOpsRungN.fss:187` now reads "For a count in 0..31, LSHIFT and RSHIFT agree with the << and >> of the same trait."; no assertion of that file changed.

38:- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. Built: F-129, which holds what runs and its open rows.
56:- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree. Still to build: walk's use of those coercions, after walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12; PLAN, phase 4).
73:- P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Built under walk, and on the compiled path for `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` with a count of the shifted value's own type. Still to build, when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library at the switch-over (P-38: the compiler's prelude is not repaired before then): the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today (gap-ledger row 442); `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare (row 383); and a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits (row 381).
77:- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they wait for a later step of their own, which no PLAN line holds yet. Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. Built.

content.content:
### 4.2 GCD and LCM

`Int.gcd`'s zero case returned its other argument unnormalized (base `Int.java:253`); it now returns the magnitude (`Int.java:292`), and the function's existing convention that `Long.MIN_VALUE` stands for `2^63` (it negates and then shifts with `>>>`) is kept. `Int$Gcd` throws when the magnitude exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (`Int.java:134-140`), `Long$Gcd` when it is negative, i.e. `2^63` (`Long.java:148-154`). `LCM` on both widths goes through one new helper, `Int.lcm` (`Int.java:274-284`), which follows the compiled body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:620-623`, `if (self = 0) OR (other = 0) then 0 else (|self| DIV (self GCD other)) DOT |other|`): zero first, then `|u / g| * |v|` by `Math.multiplyExact` (Java 8, and the JVM's own spelling of the check, as the batch record notes at `CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:35`), with the two operands whose magnitude has no `long` tested before `Math.abs`. `Int$Lcm` then range-checks to `int` (`Int.java:142-148`).

**Decision: `MIN GCD MIN` and `MIN LCM MIN` throw too.** The brief's list stops at `MIN GCD 0`, `0 GCD MIN`, `MIN LCM ±1` and `5 LCM MIN`; `MIN GCD MIN` (`2^31`, resp. `2^63`) and `MIN LCM MIN` are the same unrepresentable results reached with both operands at the minimum, measured wrapping on the base tree (`probes/IntSemProbe-before.txt:86`, `:89`, `:106`, `:109`), and the rule cannot be applied to half of them. `MIN LCM 0` is `0` (spec `:529`) and not a throw, although `MIN GCD 0` throws: the zero test comes before the divisor is computed, as in the compiled body.

**The specification's passage, read whole.** `basic-integers.tex:524-525` and `:528-529` say, besides "The result is always nonnegative", that "If either argment is 0" (for `LCM`, 1) "the result equals the other argument", which read alone gives `0 GCD -4 = -4` and `1 LCM -5 = -5`, against the first sentence. The chapter's source reconciles them: its declarations in Fortress text, kept as LaTeX comments above the rendered ones, are `opr GCD(self, other: ZZ): NN` and `opr LCM(self, other: ZZ): NN` (`:518-519`), a return type of ℕ, under which "the other argument" can only mean its magnitude. The rung follows the nonnegative reading, which is also Pavol's decision for row 334 (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:19`); the test asserts it at `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:105`, `:107`, `:124`, `:126` and `:146`.

**The unbounded `ZZ`'s `LCM` (second repair round, the skeptic's finding 2).** `BigNum$Lcm` (`BigNum.java:176-192`), bound as `ZZ`'s `LCM` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:871-872`, computed `u.divide(g).multiply(v)` with `g = u.gcd(v)` on the signed operands, so the result carried a sign and `0 LCM 0` divided by `g = 0`: `1 LCM -5` was `-5`, `-4 LCM 6` was `-12`, and `0 LCM 0` ended the run with `ArithmeticException: BigInteger divide by zero` (`probes/skeptic/SkBigLcm.walk.txt:1-4`, `:8-9`). The specification declares `GCD` and `LCM` on ℤ itself (`basic-integers.tex:520-521`), so the clause covers it. It now returns zero when either argument is zero and otherwise takes both magnitudes (`BigNum.java:178-180`) before the existing `gcd`, smaller-first swap and divide-multiply, which are unchanged; the shape is the compiled body's (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:620-623`), as `Int.lcm`'s is. The swap compared signed values before, and is meaningful only on the magnitudes it now gets. `BigInteger` has no overflow to raise, so nothing here touches how Java exceptions are mapped. `BigNum$Gcd` (`BigNum.java:170-174`) is `u.gcd(v)`, which the JVM defines nonnegative, and the skeptic's capture agrees (`probes/skeptic/SkBigLcm.walk.txt:6`). Home 1: `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:146-148` (`1 LCM -5 = 5`, `-4 LCM 6 = 12`, `0 LCM 0 = 0`), red before (`test-before-biglcm.txt`) and green after (`test-after.txt`); the skeptic's own probe now gives every wanted answer (`probes/SkBigLcm-after.txt`, no `DIFF`, `END`, exit 0). **Decision (the judge's, `JUDGE.md`, second ruling, section 2): repaired here**, rather than given an `XXX` file with row 334 left open for ℤ; the fix is four lines in a file the rung edits, and neither of the rung's stops applies.

`Int.rc` is untouched, as the brief requires (row 347 stays open). Its callers after this rung are `Int$Choose` (`Int.java:152`) and `Int$Pow` (`Int.java:225`); see section 9 on the brief's "two exponentiation callers".

### 4.3 The fixed widths, and how the count is read

Each of the four shift pairs gains one line before the existing one; `Int$LShift` (`Int.java:180-185`), for example, is `if (v < 0) return (v > -32) ? (u >> (int) -v) : (u >> 31);` followed by the original `((v & ~31) == 0) ? (u << (int) v) : 0`. The comparison with `-32` (`-64`) precedes the negation, so `Long.MIN_VALUE` is never negated. `NN32` and `NN64` shift right logically and saturate to `0` both ways (`NN32.java:184-196`, `UnsignedLong.java:185-197`).

**The `NN64` question, established.** `UnsignedLong$LShift` took its count through `UU2U`, whose `applyMethod` reads `y.getNN64()` (base `UnsignedLong.java:88-94`). Through that `long`, a negative count and a large unsigned one cannot be told apart: `FInt.getNN64` and `FLong.getNN64` return the signed value unchanged (`evaluator/values/FInt.java:36-39`, `FLong.java:37-40`), so a `ZZ32` count of `-1` and an `NN64` count of `2^64-1` both arrive as `-1L`, and `Long.MIN_VALUE` as a `ZZ64` count and `2^63` as an `NN64` count both arrive as `Long.MIN_VALUE`. **They can be told apart one step earlier, by the class of the count's value**, which is `FNN64` for an `NN64`. The same ambiguity sat in `Long$…` (`y.getLong()` of an `FNN64` is its raw bits) and in `BigNum`'s `ZL2Z`; it was harmless while every negative count saturated, and this rung's negative-count rule would have made it wrong (`-3 LSHIFT` an `NN64` count of `2^63` would have become a right shift, `-1` instead of `0`). So the count is read once, by `Int.shiftCount(FValue)` (`Int.java:261-272`): an `FNN64` of `2^63` or more as `Long.MAX_VALUE` (a count beyond every width), an `FBigNum` exactly when it fits a `long` and clamped to `Long.MIN_VALUE`/`Long.MAX_VALUE` when it does not (exact for every width, and for `ZZ`, whose values the JVM limits to `2^31-1` bits), anything else by `getLong()`. The guards are asserted at `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:73-76`.

Precedent for the shape: each natives file declares small abstract classes named for their Java types, with a shift-only one where the count's reading differs: `ZL2Z` in `Int.java:90-96` and `BigNum.java:102-108`, `NL2N` in `NN32.java:95-101`, each extended by the two shifts alone (`grep -n "extends ZL2Z\|extends NL2N"` finds only the shifts, plus the dormant `ZZ32.java`). Their `applyMethod` now calls `shiftCount`. `Long.java` and `UnsignedLong.java` had only the shared `LL2L`/`UU2U`, so each gains a shift-only twin, `LC2L` (`Long.java:104-110`) and `UC2U` (`UnsignedLong.java:96-102`), "C" for the count; the alternative, extending `NativeMeth1` directly as the `Pow` classes do (`Int.java:218-228`), was rejected to keep the four pairs one shape.

### 4.4 The unbounded ZZ

`BigNum$LShift` and `$RShift` (`BigNum.java:228-238`) call one helper, `shiftLeft(BigInteger, long)` (`BigNum.java:240-254`); `RShift` negates the count, mapping `Long.MIN_VALUE` to `Long.MAX_VALUE` first (both are beyond any `BigInteger`'s width, so the answer is the same). A negative count of magnitude up to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` is a `BigInteger.shiftRight`, a floor, as the spec's `shift` requires; beyond it the answer is `0` or `-1` by sign; zero shifted is zero; a positive count beyond `Integer.MAX_VALUE` on a nonzero value raises `IntegerOverflow` (`:246`); and a count inside the `int` range whose result `BigInteger` cannot hold is refused before the shift, by `if (u.abs().bitLength() + v > Integer.MAX_VALUE) throw Int.overflow();` (`:247`). The check is exact: `BigInteger` holds a magnitude of at most `Integer.MAX_VALUE` bits (measured with a throwaway Java probe on JDK 25 in the first round: `3 << 2147483645` succeeds with bit length `2147483647`, `3 << 2147483646` throws), and `u.abs().bitLength()` is the magnitude's bit length (for a negative power of two `u.bitLength()` alone is one less, so the `abs()` matters). `probes/PrecheckBoundary.java` measures it at the boundary for the receivers `±1`, `±3`, `±4` and `±5`, powers of two of both signs included: the check refuses exactly where `BigInteger.shiftLeft` throws, 24 cases, `mismatches 0` (`probes/PrecheckBoundary.txt:25`). Two things keep their places. The bound at `:246` stays first: `Int.shiftCount` (`Int.java:261-272`) clamps an `NN64` count of `2^63` or more and a `ZZ` count beyond a `long` to `Long.MAX_VALUE`, and without `:246` ahead of it the `long` sum `bitLength + v` would overflow, the check would pass, and `(int) v` would be `-1`, a silent right shift; `IntSemanticsRungI.fss:95` is the assertion that guards that order. And the `try`/`catch` of the JVM's `ArithmeticException` stays at `:248-253` as a backstop, because the check's exactness rests on a JDK-internal constant (`BigInteger`'s `MAX_MAG_LENGTH`).

**Why a check before the shift, measured.** The first two rounds translated the JVM's `ArithmeticException` after the call and did not check first. `BigInteger.shiftLeft` allocates the shifted magnitude before its range check throws, about 268 MB for `3 << 2147483647`. `bin/fortress` gives the JVM `-Xmx256m` when `JAVA_FLAGS` is unset (`bin/fortress:28-29`); the testSystem harness gives it 768 MB (root `build.xml:131`, `junitMem`, the `systemShard` macro's `maxmemory` at `:1181`), and the shared prefix's `JAVA_FLAGS` 4 GB. So at the launcher's own heap `:93` of the gated test ended the run with an uncatchable `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError` (`probes/skeptic/test-default-heap.txt`, the skeptic's red, reproduced in `probes/test-default-heap-before.txt`), while every run of the first two rounds, at 4 GB or 768 MB, passed. The earlier decision, "translating the JVM's own check rather than predicting it keeps the limit the JVM's", was taken without measuring at the launcher's heap, and it was wrong. The base tree fails the same way (its `u.shiftLeft((int) v)`, base `BigNum.java:224`, is the same call), so this was not a regression, but the claim of a catchable `IntegerOverflow` was the rung's. With the check, the test prints `PASS` under `bin/fortress` with `JAVA_FLAGS` unset (`test-after.txt`), and the skeptic's `SkBigAlloc.fss` prints `THROWS IntegerOverflow` at `-Xmx256m` (`probes/SkBigAlloc-after.txt`) where it ran out of memory (`probes/skeptic/SkBigAlloc.txt:1-4`). The check is the skeptic's (`probes/skeptic/fix-trial-patch.txt`), placed as the judge ruled (`JUDGE.md`, second ruling, section 1).

**What the check does not do.** A left shift whose result is representable but larger than the heap still ends the run with `OutOfMemoryError`, as any allocation beyond the heap does: `ZZ 3 LSHIFT 2147483645`, a 2^31-bit result of about 256 MB, returns at 4 GB and exhausts the 256 MB default (`probes/BigShiftHeap.txt`, from `probes/BigShiftHeap.fss`). That is the JVM's memory limit, not an integer overflow; the result fits the type, and the specification's rule (`opr-overview.tex:154-155`) does not reach it. It is not asserted.

**Decision: `IntegerOverflow`, catchable.** The brief left the exception to the rung. The alternatives were the raw `ArithmeticException` (uncatchable under `walk`, row 336's shape, and what the base tree already did for counts inside the `int` range), a `ProgramError` through `error(...)` (uncatchable, row 347's shape), or a new exception type. The spec's rule is that an integer result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow` (`opr-overview.tex:154-155`); `ZZ` has no width of its own but the JVM gives it one, and Pavol's principle is not to fight the JVM where it precludes an implementation; `IntegerOverflow` is the one exception the library has for "an integer result that does not fit". The limit is still the JVM's: the check states the boundary the JVM enforces, measured above, and the backstop translates the JVM's own exception should that boundary ever move.

### 4.5 ZZ64.narrow

`Long$FromLong` is `(int) x` (`Long.java:248-252`), as `UnsignedLong$FromLong` (`UnsignedLong.java:241-244`) and `BigNum$ToZZ32` (`BigNum.java:286-289`) already were.

## 7. The gated test that relied on the old LCM

The regression subset (section 8) turned up one red: `tests/RangePrototype.fss`, `FAIL: a dumpShow[\ZZ32\]: RightScalarRange(2,1)==...-2,-1,0,1,2] =/= a dumpShow[\ZZ32\]: LeftScalarRange(2,-1)==[2,1,0,-1,-2...;` for `(spec, curr) match for OpenScalarRange(1)==...o,o+1... and LeftScalarRange(2,-1)` (`probes/harness-regression-1.txt:6-8`). The test carries its own prototype of range intersection, `INTERSECTOLD` and `INTERSECTNEW` ("This is the current spec for INTERSECTION", `RangePrototype.fss:155`), and compares it with the library's (`:430-434`). Both prototypes compute `resultStride = this.stride LCM other.stride` (`:66`, `:171`), and `intersectUnbounded` takes its direction from the sign of `resultStride DIV other'.stride` (`:24-25`). With the old signed `LCM`, `(u / g) * v`, that quotient was `this.stride / gcd`, sign included; with `LCM` nonnegative it loses the sign whenever a stride is negative. The library does not depend on the sign: `RangeInternals.fss:513-517` flips negative strides before its `LCM`, `:442-445` restores the sign by hand, and its open-range case uses `GCD` (`:326-328`).

**Decision: the two lines now compute the signed stride the prototype means, explicitly**, `resultStride = (this.stride DIV (this.stride GCD other.stride)) DOT other.stride`, which equals the old `(u / g) * v` for the nonzero strides a range has (the `GCD` of two nonzero values is positive, and this rung does not change it there). No assertion changes; the test is green again (`probes/harness-RangePrototype.txt`, `OK (1 test)`). The alternatives were to stop (the brief lists `RangePrototype.fss:66` and `:171` under what must stay green; it does, with this edit), or to keep a signed `LCM` under `walk`, which the specification (`basic-integers.tex:528`) and Pavol's decision both rule out. `RangePrototype.fss` is a 2012-tree file and is on the `historical:` line.

## 1. What changed

`walk` applies the declared type's lifted `coerce_<T>`, found at the top level of the type's environment, in three kinds of place:
- a single function's, constructor's, method's, native's and varargs parameter (`NonPrimitive.typecheckParams` and `buildEnvFromParams`);
- an overloaded call where no overload applies without coercion: `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`, called at the team's TODO, takes the most specific applicable coercion by `conversions-coercions.tex:469-484` and refuses an ambiguous call; the result is a `Coercions.CoercedCall`, kept in the per-argument-type cache, which converts the arguments and dispatches the converted arguments as an ordinary call through the owning `OverloadedFunction` (`Coercions.java:228-230`); an overloaded method converts and calls `applyMethod` again (`OverloadedMethod.java:56-63`);
- a typed local, top-level or field declaration, and an assignment to a typed variable or field (`LHSEvaluator`, `BaseEnv.assignValue`, `BuildEnvironments`, and `LazilyEvaluatedCell`, which carries the declared type and converts when first computed).

A declaration, parameter or assignment of tuple type converts element by element, an element already of its type kept (`Coercions.coerce` and `coerceTuple`, `Coercions.java:88-116`); a size mismatch, a varargs element or an element with no coercion stays the loud error it was.

Files: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Coercions.java` (new, 271 lines); `OverloadedFunction.java` (`bestMatch`'s coercion pass, `bestMatchWithoutCoercion`, `bestMatchWithCoercion` with the ambiguity refusal); `OverloadedMethod.java`; `NonPrimitive.java`; `LHSEvaluator.java`; `BaseEnv.java`; `BuildEnvironments.java`; `env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java`.

Tests, sixteen new `.fss` files, each with one comment line pointing at this report:
- home 1, `ProjectFortress/tests/`: `CoercionCallRungC`, `CoercionOverloadRungC`, `CoercionBindRungC`, `CoercionMostSpecificRungC`, `CoercionSpecTableRungC`, `CoercionRedispatchRungC`;
- home 2, `ProjectFortress/tests/`: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`, `XXXCoercionReturnRungC`, `XXXCoercionGenericFnRungC`, `XXXCoercionGenericTraitRungC`, `XXXCoercionTupleOverloadRungC`;
- home 2, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`: `XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC` (with `CoercionAnyOverloadRungCLink.test` and `XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC.test`), `XXXCoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` (`.test`), `XXXTupleLocalVarCompiledRungC` and `XXXTupleVarFieldCompiledRungC` (each with a `.test`, linked by `TupleVarCompiledRungCLink.test`).

5:- **The re-dispatch** (the judge's ruling): the converted arguments are dispatched as an ordinary call through the owning `OverloadedFunction`, and a method call re-enters `applyMethod`. Rejected: applying the overload chosen before conversion, the first pass (section 4). Rejected: caching the choice refined by the converted type, because the type of a `coerce` result may depend on the value (`CoercionRedispatchRungC`: `g(NarrowOf(3))` = `g(Wide)` after `g(NarrowOf(2))` = `g(WideOf)`).
13:- **Tuple-typed targets** (the judge's scope decision): repaired element by element in `Coercions.coerce`, `coercionFor` unchanged. Rejected: an `XXX` test and a provisional row. Stated limits: varargs, keyword and arrow targets are not converted and not measured.
14:- **An overloaded function's tuple-typed parameter and an assignment to a tuple-typed `var` field** (the repair round's decision) are measured as not converted and given home 2 (`tests/XXXCoercionTupleOverloadRungC.fss`, row 395); the field's setter is an overloaded method (`probes/tuple-limits.txt:222`). Rejected: repairing them, which needs a second kind of per-position converter in `bestMatchWithCoercion` and a tuple rule in `Coercions.moreSpecific`, beyond the judge's instruction to leave `coercionFor` unchanged; home 3, since the specification settles it.
16:- **The compiled `XXX` check lines** follow `XXXUnionReturnRungS` (`run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` with `run_err_contains=java.lang.ClassFormatError`; the failure is at class load) and `XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC` (`run_out_contains=REACHED` with `run_err_contains=java.lang.VerifyError`), each with a plain link twin, because `FileTests` runs command tests before run tests and a run test does not compile (`FileTests.java:999-1012`; `probes/compiled-xxx-tuplevar.txt`). Not used: `run_out_contains=PASS`, which is a failure whatever the file name when unmet (`FileTests.java:534-537`, `:583-585`).
18:- **The deliberate local fix for the first `XXX` file** overlays one class, `LHSEvaluator`, compiled outside the tree (`probes/deliberate-fix.patch`): it binds a variable whose declared type is a trait of the same source file as `FAsIf` of the value, so dispatch sees `c` as a `C`, the specification's static view. A first form that wrapped every typed binding broke the library's own bindings and was narrowed. Rejected: editing the test's expected value.
## 11. What was not done

- Coercion at a declared return type (row 387), at a generic function's declared parameter (row 388), for a generic trait's coercion (row 389), at an overloaded function's tuple-typed parameter and a tuple-typed field assignment (row 395): not repaired under `walk`, each gated as an expected failure. Varargs, keyword and arrow targets: not converted and not measured. A `coerce` declared from a tuple type, applied at a single-parameter overload given several arguments: not measured (`fixupArgCount` packs them into one tuple, and the re-dispatch then carries the packed tuple).
- Tests and properties are not measurable: the checker refuses `test` and `property` on both paths (`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, § The territory map, the entry on `IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`). Contracts are not measurable without a line of `Library/`. Subexpressions other than assignment were not measured. Generic inference over mixed widths (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/price-keep-the-rule.md:88`) is not measured beyond row 388's single case.
- `OverloadedMethod.getApplicableMethod` (`:47-53`) still casts to `MethodClosure`; it is reached only with arguments already converted, and no case was found in which a refinement needs a coercion that the top-level choice did not make.
- Rows 396 and 397 are compiled-path code-generation defects outside the rung's files.
- `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` were not run, per the brief; the checker-count stage was not run, its inputs (the compiled checker and `Library/`) being untouched, so it stays at 103.

\section{Coercions for Tuple and Arrow Types}
\seclabel{coercion-tuple-arrow}

Unlike other types, tuple types (described in \secref{tuple-types}) and
arrow types (described in \secref{arrow-types}) are
not defined explicitly.  Therefore coercions to these types are also
not defined explicitly.  Instead, the following rules describe when
these coercions are implicitly defined.

There is a coercion from a tuple type $\VAR{X}$ to a tuple type
$\VAR{Y}$ if all the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\VAR{X}$ is not a subtype of $\VAR{Y}$;

content.content:
$\VAR{X}$ is not a subtype of $\VAR{Y}$;
\item
for every plain type $\VAR{T}$ in $\VAR{Y}$, there is a corresponding
plain type in $\VAR{X}$ whose type is substitutable for $\VAR{T}$;
\item
if neither $\VAR{X}$ nor $\VAR{Y}$ has a varargs type, then they have
the same number of plain types;
\item
if $\VAR{X}$ has a varargs type, then $\VAR{Y}$ has a varargs type,
the type $\VAR{S}$ of the varargs type $\VAR{S}...$ in $\VAR{X}$ is
substitutable for the type $\VAR{T}$ of the varargs type
$\VAR{T}...$ in $\VAR{Y}$, and $\VAR{X}$ and $\VAR{Y}$ have the same
number of plain types;
\item
if $\VAR{X}$ has no varargs type and $\VAR{Y}$ has a varargs type
$\VAR{T}...$, then every plain type in $\VAR{X}$ that has no
corresponding plain type in $\VAR{Y}$ is substitutable for $\VAR{T}$; and
\item
the correspondence between keyword-type pairs in $\VAR{X}$ and
$\VAR{Y}$ is bijective, and the type of each such pair in $\VAR{X}$ is
substitutable for the type in the corresponding pair in $\VAR{Y}$.
\end{enumerate}

Tuple type coercions are invoked by distributing the coercion
elementwise.  However, if an element type of the tuple type being coerced
from is a subtype of the corresponding element type of the tuple type being
coerced to, the coercion is ignored.  For example, the following coercions:
%coerce_[\(A, B)\](x, y)
%coerce_[\(kwd=A)\](kwd=x)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket(A, B)\rrbracket(x, y)\)\\
\(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket(\VAR{kwd}=A)\rrbracket(\VAR{kwd}=x)\)
\end{Fortress}
are rewritten to:
%(coerce_[\A\](x), coerce_[\B\](y))
%(coerce_[\(kwd=A)\](x))
\begin{Fortress}
\((\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{}A\rrbracket(x), \mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{}B\rrbracket(y))\)\\
\((\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket(\VAR{kwd}=A)\rrbracket(x))\)
\end{Fortress}
However, if the type of \VAR{y} were a subtype of \VAR{B} then the
first coercion would instead be rewritten to:
%(coerce_[\A\](x), y)
\begin{Fortress}
\((\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{}A\rrbracket(x), y)\)
\end{Fortress}

Coercions to varargs types such as the following:
%coerce_[\(A...)\](x, y)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket(A\ldots)\rrbracket(x, y)\)
\end{Fortress}
are invoked by applying the coercion to the type in the varargs type,
\VAR{A} in this example, to each of the elements of the tuple.
Additionally, there is a coercion from any type \VAR{T} to a tuple type
solely with varargs type \EXP{(T\ldots)}.
